title: What Type of Learner Are You?
subtitle: A 3-minute study-habit check for Class 10 & 12.
_note: Study-HABIT types (what you do today), not fixed learning styles: the visual/auditory idea is not supported by research (site rule: no pseudo-science). Each option key is one of the 5 profiles; the option order varies per question on purpose. Copy deck: Board2027_Copy_Deck.md section 2.
disclaimer: This is your study habit today, not how your brain is wired. Habits can change, and the workshop shows you how.

cta.title: 🎓 Board exam 2027? Change the habit in 3 LIVE days
cta.text: The free 3-day LIVE workshop for Class 10 & 12 shows you, step by step, how to remember faster, solve maths questions on your own and build your own study routine.

questions.text: You sit down to study a new chapter. What do you usually do first?

options.text: Read it two or three times and highlight the important lines
Read one section, close the book and write down what I remember
Go straight to the solved examples and the teacher's notes
Skim it for now; I'll study it properly closer to the test
Start reading, then drift into a 'but why does this happen?' tangent

questions.text: You're stuck on a maths question. What happens next?

options.text: I look at the solution, it makes sense, and I move on
I think about it for a while, then end up on my phone
I re-read the theory and the examples in the chapter
I try for a few minutes, write what I know, then check a hint
I skip it for now; I'll deal with it before the exam

questions.text: When do you usually revise a chapter?

options.text: Mostly the night before the test
A day later, then a few days later, then again after a week
Whenever I get time, by reading my notes again
When I feel like it; there's no fixed time
When the teacher revises it in class or tuition

questions.text: What breaks your focus most often while you study?

options.text: My phone, or my own thoughts wandering to other questions
Reading the same page again gets boring and I lose interest
I get stuck and wait for someone to explain it
Not much: I study in short, timed blocks with the phone away
Nothing much until the night before the exam, then panic

questions.text: In a tuition or coaching test, what usually happens?

options.text: The page looked familiar while reading, but my mind goes blank
I remember what I crammed last night, but not the older chapters
Most of it comes back, because I have practised recalling it
I understood it in class, but I can't start the question on my own
I know the ideas, but I lose time and don't finish

questions.text: How do you decide that you have 'learnt' a topic?

options.text: It made sense when the teacher explained it
It looks familiar when I read it
I get the big idea, even if I can't write the details
I could say it out loud right before the test
I can answer questions on it with the book closed
Short question lists I can quiz myself with
Full of highlighting and underlining
Unfinished; I plan to complete them before the exam
Solutions copied from the board or the solution book
Full of side questions and doodles, but hard to revise from

questions.text: A week after a test, how much of that chapter do you still remember?

options.text: Very little; most of it is gone
The interesting parts, not the boring details
I recognise the method when I see it, but can't start alone
Most of it, because I keep revising it at gaps
It feels familiar, but I couldn't write it out

questions.text: You have two hours to study tonight. What does it usually look like?

options.text: Reading and highlighting the chapter again
Watching a video or reading solved examples
Short focus blocks: test myself, check, fix the gaps
I start well, but the phone and other thoughts take over
Not much tonight; I'll do one long session before the test

questions.text: A friend asks you to explain a topic you studied last week. What happens?

options.text: I explain the 'why' with excitement, then go off topic
I can explain most of it and I notice where I'm unsure
I would have to cram it again first
I need to open my notes first
I can follow it with the solution in front of me, not from scratch

Re-Reader.name: The Re-Reader
Re-Reader.description: You read and highlight again and again. The page starts to feel familiar, so it feels like learning, but in the test your mind goes blank. Familiar is not the same as remembered: recalling it on your own is what makes it stick.
steps: After each page, close the book and write down what you remember.
Open the book and check: tick what you got right and fill in what you missed.
Next time, start with the gaps. This is called active recall.

Last-Minute Crammer.name: The Last-Minute Crammer
Last-Minute Crammer.description: You can study hard the night before, and it often gets you through the next day. But most of it is gone a week later, so older chapters keep slipping away before the board exam.
steps: Revise each topic again 1 day after you first study it.
Then revise it after 3 days, and again after 7 days. Short revisions are enough.
Write these dates in a small calendar so revision is not left for the last night. This is spaced repetition.

Solution Watcher.name: The Solution Watcher
Solution Watcher.description: When the teacher solves a question, everything makes sense. On your own, you can't start the same question. Watching someone solve it gives understanding; solving it yourself is what works in the exam.
steps: Try every question on your own for 5 minutes before you look at the solution.
If you are stuck, write the question in your own words and write down what you already know.
After reading the solution, close it and solve the question again yourself.

Deep-Thinking Drifter.name: The Deep-Thinking Drifter
Deep-Thinking Drifter.description: You ask big 'why' questions, and that curiosity is a real strength. But your focus breaks, the phone wins, and the work in front of you doesn't get finished.
steps: Keep a 'question parking' notebook: write the big question down and come back to it later.
Study in 25-minute focus blocks with a short break after each one.
Keep your phone in another room while you study.

Self-Tester.name: The Self-Tester
Self-Tester.description: You already test yourself and space out your revision. That is how memory gets stronger. Your next step is to make your practice closer to the real exam.
steps: Mix questions from different chapters in one practice session.
Time yourself, the way the exam will.
Explain each topic to someone in simple words (the Feynman Technique) and notice where you get stuck.
